title: Previous governments have engaged in ‘cover-up’ over harm done to nuclear test veterans, says defence secretary – UK politics live
description:
Wes Streeting said he believes a review will help ensure that ‘the cover-up is exposed’

Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, has said previous governments have engaged in a cover-up over the harm done to veterans who were involved in nuclear tests in the 1950s and 1960s.

The government has launched a Hillsborough-style investigation to establish what happened. This is something campaigners have been seeking for decades.

Well, we’re not going to prejudge the panel, but it’s got to lead where the facts take them. It’s got to proceed without fear or favour, and then we’ve got to act on its findings, just as we did with Hillsborough …

I think the power of what Bishop James Jones [who is leading the review] will do will help us to make sure that the cover-up is exposed.

If it looks like a duck, quacks like a duck.
text: Streeting says there has been 'cover-up' over harm done to nuclear test veterans, as inquiry launched
Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, has said previous governments have engaged in a cover-up over the harm done to veterans who were involved in nuclear tests in the 1950s and 1960s.
The government has launched a Hillsborough-style investigation to establish what happened. This is something campaigners have been seeking for decades.
On Newsnight last night, in a programme focusing on the announcement, Streeting was asked if the government was prepared to make an apology or pay compensation to those affected. He replied:

double quotation markWell, we’re not going to prejudge the panel, but it’s got to lead where the facts take them. It’s got to proceed without fear or favour, and then we’ve got to act on its findings, just as we did with Hillsborough … I think the power of what Bishop James Jones [who is leading the review] will do will help us to make sure that the cover-up is exposed.
Asked to confirm he was saying it was a cover-up, Streeting responded:
double quotation markIf it looks like a duck, quacks like a duck.
John Swinney says Burnham must honour Labour promise to cut energy bills by £300
John Swinney, the Scottish first minister, is also urging Andy Burnham to step in to bring energy bills down after Ofgem announced the price cap will rise by 26% in January. (See 9.41am.)
In a statement, Swinney said:

double quotation markHigh energy bills are already causing real hardship across Scotland and confirmation of a £443 increase in January, when the new price cap comes into effect, will be causing understandable anxiety for many people. Scotland’s energy is projected to send an additional £2.6bn in revenue to the Treasury next year – and yet people in Scotland are set to see bills increase even further. We are one of the most energy-rich nations in the world and yet we pay some of the highest bills in Europe – it does not add up. The UK government came to office promising to cut energy bills by £300 – but bills are already about £300 higher and are set to rise further in January. We need to see the prime minister deliver on that promise and urgently set out how he will bring bills down substantially.

Before the 2024 general election, Labour said its plans to create GB Energy would bring down energy bills by £300. That figure was based on this research from Ember, an energy thinktank, about the impact of switching to clean energy electricity production by 2030 (a Labour pledge). The figure was meant to mean that energy bills would be £300 lower than the figure they otherwise would be without the transition. But this nuance did not survive as the figure became a headline pledge, and it was widely – though wrongly – assumed to mean Labour was promising to cut bills by £300 from their 2024 level.
Home Office says more offenders to be tagged before they leave prison
Thousands more offenders will be tagged before leaving prison in a bid to tighten supervision of those released, the Press Association reports. PA says:

double quotation markThe move expands on a pilot scheme to fit eligible offenders with GPS, alcohol and curfew tags before they leave the prison gates, rather than sending them off with a tagging order in place. It comes as further waves of offenders are set to be released early over the next year to free up prison spaces in overcrowded jails in England and Wales. Six prisons started fitting tags before departure last year under the “tagging at source” scheme, and more will follow suit to bring the number to 83 by the end of March.
Announcing the move, Alex Norris, the justice secretary, said:

double quotation markCriminals and defendants should be under no illusion that leaving prison or court means escaping the watchful eye of the authorities. Tagging is just one of the many tools we use to monitor offenders, but the evidence shows it works. By fitting tags before they even walk through the prison gates or out of court, we’re tightening the net around those who break the law and making sure there is nowhere to hide from the consequences of their actions.
Phillipson backs Burnham engaging with social media influencers

Bridget Phillipson, the minister for women and equalities, has defended Andy Burnham’s engagement with online influencers in the light of the controversy over TikToker posting a “bomboclaat pussywagon” video filmed outside No 10.
Asked about the row on BBC Breakfast, Phillipson said:

double quotation markWe can’t control everything that people say or do, but I am not happy with that video. I’m glad it’s been taken down, but it was totally unacceptable. What I do think is right, however, is that as well as politicians like me coming on your programme to reach all of your viewers, that we seek to reach a wide audience through all of those people that will consume their media, their news on social media platforms, on podcasts. We want to reach people where they are. That’s what the prime minister is seeking to do.
Burnham urged to step in to halt energy bill hikes in January, as Ofgem says price cap to rise 26%

Millions of British households will face annual energy bills of more than £2,000 a year for the first time since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, as the cap on energy bills climbs for a third straight quarter, Jillian Ambrose reports.
Commenting on the increase for the Conservatives, Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy secretary, said:

double quotation markIt is an outrage that, as bills soar, Labour are not only piling green levies and taxes on to bills but signing us up to an EU scheme that risks pushing them even higher. Labour are utterly out of touch and could fix this tomorrow if they had the backbone.
And Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, said:

double quotation markRight now, millions of families feel completely powerless in the face of reckless wars driving up energy prices, and they are being left to fend for themselves while bills spiral out of control. The meagre and poorly targeted support the government has promised will be wiped out by this rise, and many of those who most desperately need help won’t get a penny. The government needs to wake up to the scale of this crisis. The prime minister must step in and stop such a massive hike going ahead in January. The Treasury and the energy network companies are both raking in huge windfalls because of this crisis - that cash should be used to keep bills down for struggling households, not left sitting in Treasury coffers and shareholders’ pockets.
Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, said:
double quotation markLabour and the Tories net zero obsession is going to bankrupt Britain.
And Zack Polanski, the Green party leader, said:

double quotation markWe’re paying the price for Trump’s war in Iran & our failure to get off the fossil fuel rollercoaster coaster The UK supported that war, with US bombers launching from here And early signs from Burnham (Jackdaw, warm home, elec vehicles) are fossil fuels are here to stay.

double quotation markIt doesn’t have to be like this. We could transform our economy to be entirely based on clean, affordable energy. And we could ban the US from using our bases for good, and end our tacit support for their wars of aggression.
Julia Kollewe has more on this story on the business live blog.
Burnham’s devolution plans risk ‘significant disparities’ for people in England, MPs say
Good morning. Kemi Badenoch will be choosing what to raise at PMQs this morning and she’s spoilt for choice.
It would be very surprising if she did not raise the most important story of the morning – the news that gas and electricity prices will rise by 26% from January under Ofgem’s latest price cap.

But Badenoch is also interested in welfare spending, and yesterday’s publication of the Timms report has left MPs still puzzling about what the government will propose for benefits reform when it publishes its white paper next year.
Burnham himself has two announcements of his own today.

He has launched a Hillsborough-style investigation to examine a programme of blood tests on service personnel during nuclear weapons trials, which he said had been the subject of a “criminal cover-up on an industrial scale”.
And he has called recent high-profile rape trials a “watershed moment” for the UK and has opened the door to a wider ban on non-disclosure agreements.

And, as someone who is herself over-focused on social media, it is likely that Badenoch will also want to raise the row about TikTok influencers in Downing Street. It is a story about preposterous media figures with no respect for the political establishment; but that’s enough about tabloid editors for now.

One thing unlikely to come up is the public accounts committee report out today on devolving power in England. So let’s give it some coverage anyway. Burnham has many political ambitions, but the one idea that seems to matter to him more than any other, and that marks him out from his predecessors, is his desire to devolve power out of Westminster, to let mayors and other local leaders have more clout and – via this devolution – to promote growth “in every postcode”.
But, given the way the policy is being implemented, this may not happen, says the committee, which has a Labour majority. It says:

double quotation markThere is a risk of significant disparities in opportunities and outcomes for people living in different parts of England, depending on what type of strategic authority they have. The government has consciously adopted a differentiated approach to devolution. Areas that choose an elected mayor to lead their strategic authority (‘mayoral strategic authorities’) can access a broader range of devolved powers and funding flexibilities to improve local outcomes than those without a mayor. However, even among areas with a mayor, powers and arrangements differ. Only seven of England’s 18 mayoral strategic authorities receive an integrated settlement – a single funding pot for each area, collectively worth around £15.9bn up to 2029–30, that provides greater funding flexibilities and multi-year funding certainty. London also differs from other mayoral areas. Its constituent boroughs have no formal role in the Greater London Authority’s decisions or vote on its budget. This risks decisions being taken without formal input from the boroughs that are responsible for delivering local services, and may make lines of accountability less clear for local people. Fiscal devolution could further deepen differences between areas. The government’s October 2026 Fiscal Devolution Roadmap confirms that only mayoral strategic authorities will be able to retain a share of local income tax. It proposes ways to limit disparities between different mayoral strategic authorities, but important details are still to be determined, including through the next spending review, and it therefore remains uncertain how effective these arrangements will be.
Here is the agenda for the day.
Noon: Andy Burnham faces Kemi Badenoch at PMQs.
3pm: Nigel Farage and Arron Banks launch their Keep Britain Out campaign opposing the idea of the UK rejoining the EU.
